claim: Classical models of cerebellar learning posit that climbing fibers operate according to a supervised learning rule to instruct changes in motor output by signaling the occurrence of movement errors.
source: Classical models of cerebellar learning posit that climbing fibers operate according to a supervised learning rule to instruct changes in motor output by signaling the occurrence of movement errors.
evidence: This is a statement about established models in the field, supported by citations to foundational work (Albus, 1971; Ito, 1972; Marr, 1969) mentioned later in the text.

claim: Cerebellar output is associated with non-motor behaviors.
source: However, cerebellar output is also associated with non-motor behaviors, and recently with modulating reward association pathways in the VTA.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research mentioned in the introduction.

claim: The cerebellum modulates reward association pathways in the VTA.
source: However, cerebellar output is also associated with non-motor behaviors, and recently with modulating reward association pathways in the VTA.
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent work (Carta et al., 2019) mentioned in the discussion.

claim: Distinct climbing fiber responses exist in three lateral cerebellar regions that can each signal reward prediction.
source: We find distinct climbing fiber responses in three lateral cerebellar regions that can each signal reward prediction.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data presented in Figures 2-6.

claim: The cerebellum contributes significantly to many non-motor processes such as cognition.
source: However, it is becoming widely appreciated that the cerebellum also contributes significantly to many non-motor processes (Schmahmann, 1991) such as cognition (Kim et al., 1994), social processing (Van Overwalle et al., 2014), aggression (Reis et al., 1973) and emotion (Schmahmann and Caplan, 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The cerebellum contributes significantly to social processing.
source: However, it is becoming widely appreciated that the cerebellum also contributes significantly to many non-motor processes (Schmahmann, 1991) such as cognition (Kim et al., 1994), social processing (Van Overwalle et al., 2014), aggression (Reis et al., 1973) and emotion (Schmahmann and Caplan, 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Van Overwalle et al., 2014.

claim: The cerebellum contributes significantly to aggression.
source: However, it is becoming widely appreciated that the cerebellum also contributes significantly to many non-motor processes (Schmahmann, 1991) such as cognition (Kim et al., 1994), social processing (Van Overwalle et al., 2014), aggression (Reis et al., 1973) and emotion (Schmahmann and Caplan, 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Reis et al., 1973.

claim: The cerebellum contributes significantly to emotion.
source: However, it is becoming widely appreciated that the cerebellum also contributes significantly to many non-motor processes (Schmahmann, 1991) such as cognition (Kim et al., 1994), social processing (Van Overwalle et al., 2014), aggression (Reis et al., 1973) and emotion (Schmahmann and Caplan, 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Schmahmann and Caplan, 2006.

claim: Cerebellar deficits are associated with autism spectrum disorders.
source: Moreover, cerebellar deficits are associated with non-motor conditions including autism spectrum disorders (Wang et al., 2014), deficits of language processing and vocal learning (Ackermann, 2008), schizophrenia (Mothersill et al., 2016) and other impairments (Ivry and Spencer, 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2014.

claim: Cerebellar deficits are associated with deficits of language processing and vocal learning.
source: Moreover, cerebellar deficits are associated with non-motor conditions including autism spectrum disorders (Wang et al., 2014), deficits of language processing and vocal learning (Ackermann, 2008), schizophrenia (Mothersill et al., 2016) and other impairments (Ivry and Spencer, 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Ackermann, 2008.

claim: Cerebellar deficits are associated with schizophrenia.
source: Moreover, cerebellar deficits are associated with non-motor conditions including autism spectrum disorders (Wang et al., 2014), deficits of language processing and vocal learning (Ackermann, 2008), schizophrenia (Mothersill et al., 2016) and other impairments (Ivry and Spencer, 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Mothersill et al., 2016.

claim: Cerebellar learning is instructed by signals carried by climbing fibers from the inferior olive.
source: Classical models posit that cerebellar learning is instructed by signals carried by an afferent fiber projection from the inferior olive called climbing fibers (Albus, 1971; Ito, 1972; Marr, 1969).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to classical models (Albus, 1971; Ito, 1972; Marr, 1969).

claim: Climbing fibers exhibit a wide range of responses distinct from motor error signals.
source: In line with this view, accumulating evidence has demonstrated a wide range of climbing fiber responses that are distinct from motor error signals (Kitazawa et al., 1998; Streng et al., 2017), including temporal-difference error signals (Ohmae and Medina, 2015) and reward prediction signals (Heffley et al., 2018; Kostadinov et al., 2019; Larry et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Climbing fibers can exhibit temporal-difference error signals.
source: In line with this view, accumulating evidence has demonstrated a wide range of climbing fiber responses that are distinct from motor error signals (Kitazawa et al., 1998; Streng et al., 2017), including temporal-difference error signals (Ohmae and Medina, 2015) and reward prediction signals (Heffley et al., 2018; Kostadinov et al., 2019; Larry et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Ohmae and Medina, 2015.

claim: Climbing fibers can exhibit reward prediction signals.
source: In line with this view, accumulating evidence has demonstrated a wide range of climbing fiber responses that are distinct from motor error signals (Kitazawa et al., 1998; Streng et al., 2017), including temporal-difference error signals (Ohmae and Medina, 2015) and reward prediction signals (Heffley et al., 2018; Kostadinov et al., 2019; Larry et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Heffley et al., 2018; Kostadinov et al., 2019; Larry et al., 2019.

claim: A disynaptic pathway exists from the lateral cerebellum to the striatum.
source: Rabies tracing experiments have identified a disynaptic pathway from the lateral cerebellum to the striatum (Hoshi et al., 2005), and recent functional connectivity experiments have revealed a direct, monosynaptic connection from the lateral cerebellum to the ventral tegmental area (VTA) (Carta et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Hoshi et al., 2005.

claim: A direct, monosynaptic connection exists from the lateral cerebellum to the ventral tegmental area (VTA).
source: Rabies tracing experiments have identified a disynaptic pathway from the lateral cerebellum to the striatum (Hoshi et al., 2005), and recent functional connectivity experiments have revealed a direct, monosynaptic connection from the lateral cerebellum to the ventral tegmental area (VTA) (Carta et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Carta et al., 2019.

claim: Lateral cerebellar output can modulate reward-driven behaviors.
source: These experiments also showed that lateral cerebellar output can modulate reward-driven behaviors by the same pathway.
evidence: This statement refers to experiments by Carta et al., 2019 mentioned in the previous sentence.

claim: Cerebellar granule cells can display reward related signals.
source: Indeed, there is evidence that cerebellar granule cells can display reward related signals (Wagner et al., 2017), and climbing fibers can display signals consistent with reward prediction errors in certain behaviors (Heffley et al., 2018; Kostadinov et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Wagner et al., 2017.

claim: Climbing fibers can display signals consistent with reward prediction errors in certain behaviors.
source: Indeed, there is evidence that cerebellar granule cells can display reward related signals (Wagner et al., 2017), and climbing fibers can display signals consistent with reward prediction errors in certain behaviors (Heffley et al., 2018; Kostadinov et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Heffley et al., 2018; Kostadinov et al., 2019.

claim: Mice learned the association between the visual cue and the timing of reward delivery after multiple training sessions (mean = 5.7 ± 0.4 days).
source: After multiple training sessions (mean = 5.7 ± 0.4 days), mice learned the association between the visual cue and the time of reward delivery, significantly reducing both their reaction times (Day 1, 742.8 ± 25.4 ms; Day N+1, 544.7 ± 13.0 ms; p=8.52 × 10−8, n = 27 mice, paired t-test, Figure 1E) and miss rates (Day 1, 0.39 ± 0.04; Day N+1, 0.03 ± 0.01; p=6.37 × 10−9, paired t-test, Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data showing significant changes in reaction times and miss rates, presented in Figure 1E and 1F.

claim: Mice significantly reduced their reaction times after learning (Day 1: 742.8 ± 25.4 ms; Day N+1: 544.7 ± 13.0 ms; p=8.52 × 10−8).
source: After multiple training sessions (mean = 5.7 ± 0.4 days), mice learned the association between the visual cue and the time of reward delivery, significantly reducing both their reaction times (Day 1, 742.8 ± 25.4 ms; Day N+1, 544.7 ± 13.0 ms; p=8.52 × 10−8, n = 27 mice, paired t-test, Figure 1E) and miss rates (Day 1, 0.39 ± 0.04; Day N+1, 0.03 ± 0.01; p=6.37 × 10−9, paired t-test, Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral measurements and statistical analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Mice significantly reduced their miss rates after learning (Day 1: 0.39 ± 0.04; Day N+1: 0.03 ± 0.01; p=6.37 × 10−9).
source: After multiple training sessions (mean = 5.7 ± 0.4 days), mice learned the association between the visual cue and the time of reward delivery, significantly reducing both their reaction times (Day 1, 742.8 ± 25.4 ms; Day N+1, 544.7 ± 13.0 ms; p=8.52 × 10−8, n = 27 mice, paired t-test, Figure 1E) and miss rates (Day 1, 0.39 ± 0.04; Day N+1, 0.03 ± 0.01; p=6.37 × 10−9, paired t-test, Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral measurements and statistical analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Mice developed robust licking responses following the visual cue on omission trials after learning that were absent in naïve animals.
source: In addition to developing well-timed licking responses that approximated the time of reward delivery on rewarded trials, mice also developed robust licking responses following the visual cue on omission trials after learning that were absent in naïve animals (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: There was a significant increase in Cspk activity following reward delivery in naïve animals in lobule simplex (n = 308 trials, five mice, p=5×10−19).
source: Using this approach, we observed a significant increase in the Cspk activity following reward delivery in naïve animals (n = 308 trials, five mice, p=5×10−19, paired t-test), but no significant response on reward omission trials (n = 74 trials, five mice, p=0.595, paired t-test) (Figure 2B, top).
evidence: This is supported by mesoscale calcium imaging data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: There was no significant Cspk response on reward omission trials in naïve animals in lobule simplex (n = 74 trials, five mice, p=0.595).
source: Using this approach, we observed a significant increase in the Cspk activity following reward delivery in naïve animals (n = 308 trials, five mice, p=5×10−19, paired t-test), but no significant response on reward omission trials (n = 74 trials, five mice, p=0.595, paired t-test) (Figure 2B, top).
evidence: This is supported by mesoscale calcium imaging data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: After learning, significant Cspk responses were maintained in lobule simplex (n = 749 trials, six mice, p=3.3×10−100).
source: After learning, significant Cspk responses were maintained (n = 749 trials, six mice, p=3.3×10−100, paired t-test), but were shifted in time, and preceded reward delivery on rewarded trials (Figure 2B, bottom, Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by mesoscale calcium imaging data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2B and 2C.

claim: After learning, Cspk responses were shifted in time and preceded reward delivery on rewarded trials in lobule simplex.
source: After learning, significant Cspk responses were maintained (n = 749 trials, six mice, p=3.3×10−100, paired t-test), but were shifted in time, and preceded reward delivery on rewarded trials (Figure 2B, bottom, Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by mesoscale calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2B and 2C.

claim: After learning, there was a significant Cspk response on omission trials preceding reward delivery in lobule simplex (n = 156 trials, six mice, p=5.4×10−16).
source: Moreover, after learning there was also a significant response on omission trials preceding reward delivery (n = 156 trials, six mice, p=5.4×10−16, paired t-test) (Figure 2B, bottom, Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by mesoscale calcium imaging data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2B and 2D.

claim: The latency of Cspk activity decreased significantly across learning in lobule simplex (n = 6 mice, p=1.04 × 10−6).
source: Across experiments, the latency of Cspk activity decreased significantly (n = 6 mice, p=1.04 × 10−6, paired t-test) (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of Cspk latency data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The shift in Cspk timing (ΔCspk = 441 ms) was greater than the change in lick timing (Δlick = 185 ms).
source: Notably, this shift in Cspk timing (ΔCspk = 441 ms) was greater than the change in lick timing (Δlick = 185 ms), indicating that the Cspk response did not simply follow the timing of motor output.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of timing measurements from the data.

claim: Cspk responses after learning had the same timing for rewarded and omission trials in lobule simplex (Rewarded trial latency = 383 ± 15 ms, Omission trial latency = 378 ± 19 ms, n = 6 mice, p=0.78 × 10−6).
source: In addition, we find that Cspk responses after learning had the same timing for rewarded and omission trials (Rewarded trial latency = 383 ± 15 ms, Omission trial latency = 378 ± 19 ms, n = 6 mice, p=0.78 × 10−6, paired t test) (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by timing analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: When reward was delivered unexpectedly after learning, Cspk activity followed reward delivery and was significantly delayed compared with rewarded trials (Day N+2; rewarded trial latency = 366.1 ± 31 ms, unexpected trial latency 793 ± 31 ms, n = 5 mice, p=2.40 × 10−4).
source: In contrast, when reward was delivered unexpectedly after learning (i.e. in absence of the visual cue), Cspk activity followed reward delivery, and was significantly delayed compared with rewarded trials (Day N+2; rewarded trial latency = 366.1 ± 31 ms, unexpected trial latency 793 ± 31 ms, n = 5 mice, p=2.40 × 10−4, paired t-test).
evidence: This is supported by timing analysis of Cspk responses to unexpected reward.

claim: The latency of Cspk responses on unexpected reward trials was equivalent to the timing of responses to rewarded trials in naïve animals (p=0.38).
source: The latency of Cspk responses on unexpected reward trials was, however, equivalent to the timing of responses to rewarded trials in naïve animals (p=0.38, two-sample t-test) (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of timing data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: In lobule simplex, significantly elevated Cspk rates were observed following reward delivery in naïve animals (n = 1040 dendrites, 15 mice, p=5.5×10−48).
source: As in our mesoscale imaging experiments, these data revealed significantly elevated Cspk rates following reward delivery in naïve animals (n = 1040 dendrites, 15 mice, p=5.5×10−48, one-tailed t-test) (Figure 3A,D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1) but no significant response during this window on omission trials (p=0.98).
evidence: This is supported by two-photon imaging data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3A, 3D, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: In lobule simplex, there was no significant Cspk response on omission trials in naïve animals (p=0.98).
source: As in our mesoscale imaging experiments, these data revealed significantly elevated Cspk rates following reward delivery in naïve animals (n = 1040 dendrites, 15 mice, p=5.5×10−48, one-tailed t-test) (Figure 3A,D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1) but no significant response during this window on omission trials (p=0.98).
evidence: This is supported by two-photon imaging data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3A and 3D.

claim: After learning in lobule simplex, significantly elevated Cspk rates were observed prior to reward delivery on both rewarded (n = 906 dendrites, 16 mice, p=2.3×10−60) and omission trials (p=1.4×10−33).
source: After learning, we observed significantly elevated Cspk rates prior to reward delivery on both rewarded (n = 906 dendrites, 16 mice, p=2.3×10−60, one-tailed t-test) and omission trials (p=1.4×10−33) that were comparable across trial types (p=0.01, paired t-test; Figure 3B,C,E).
evidence: This is supported by two-photon imaging data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3B, 3C, and 3E.

claim: After learning in lobule simplex, post-reward Cspk rates were significantly reduced (p=2.0×10−19).
source: In addition, post-reward Cspk rates were significantly reduced after learning (p=2.0×10−19, unpaired t-test), with small elevations in spiking (reward trials: p=3.3×10−4; omission trials: p=6.7×10−6; one-tailed t-test) that were equivalent on both rewarded and omission trials (p=0.46; paired t-test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of two-photon imaging data.

claim: There were no Cspk responses that were reliably suppressed below baseline after the time of expected reward on omission trials in lobule simplex.
source: Notably, there were no Cspk responses that were reliably suppressed below baseline after the time of expected reward on omission trials (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is based on analysis of two-photon imaging data as described in the methods.

claim: A small subset of PC dendrites (n = 204/906 dendrites) in lobule simplex exhibited significant post-reward responses and also responded following the visual cue after learning (p=5.9×10−36).
source: To test whether unique populations of PC dendrites exhibit Cspk responses to reward and following the visual cue after learning, we identified the subset of PC dendrites with significant post-reward responses (n = 204/906 dendrites; Figure 3—figure supplement 2). This small subset of PC dendrites also responded following the visual cue (p=5.9×10−36; one-tailed t-test), indicating that a minority of PC dendrites can exhibit Cspk responses to both reward and the visual cue after learning.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of two-photon imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The majority of PC dendrites (n = 702/906 dendrites) in lobule simplex did not respond to the reward after learning, and instead only responded to the reward-predicting cue (p=3.9×10−36).
source: However, the majority of PC dendrites (n = 702/906 dendrites) did not respond to the reward after learning, and instead only responded to the reward-predicting cue (p=3.9×10−36, one-tailed t-test; Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of two-photon imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: In lobule simplex, on trials where reward was delivered unexpectedly after learning, Cspk rates increased significantly after the time of unexpected reward delivery (n = 243 dendrites; six mice, p=1.6×10−8).
source: To disambiguate Cspk responses related to reward versus reward expectation, we measured responses to unexpected reward after learning (Day N+2). On these trials, Cspk rates increased significantly after the time of unexpected reward delivery (n = 243 dendrites; six mice, p=1.6×10−8, one-tailed t-test; Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by two-photon imaging data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claim: After an additional day of training in lobule simplex, there was no longer a significant post-reward response on trials where reward was expected (p=0.8).
source: Moreover, with this additional day of training, there was no longer a significant post-reward response on trials where reward was expected (p=0.8).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of two-photon imaging data.

claim: In lobule simplex, Cspk rates increased significantly prior to reward delivery when reward was expected (p=1.2×10−12).
source: In the same experiments, Cspk rates increased significantly prior to reward delivery when reward was expected (p=1.2×10−12, one-tailed t-test; Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by two-photon imaging data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claim: In lobule simplex, PC dendrites that were significantly responsive following the reward-predicting cue (n = 84/243 dendrites) were also significantly responsive after the unexpected reward (p=2.3×10−12).
source: Notably, the PC dendrites that were significantly responsive following the reward-predicting cue (n = 84/243 dendrites), were also significantly responsive after the unexpected reward (p=2.3×1012, one-tailed t-test; Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of two-photon imaging data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: In lobule simplex, there was no significant Cspk response to licking during the inter-trial interval (p=0.6; n = 768 dendrites, 13 mice).
source: To directly assess the role of licking in modulating Cspk rates, we first generated a lick-triggered average of Cspk activity from licks generated during the inter-trial interval (ITI). These data revealed no significant Cspk response to licking (p=0.6; n = 768 dendrites, 13 mice, one-tailed t-test; Figure 3H), consistent with previous reports showing a lack of lick-related Cspk activity in area LS (Bryant et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by lick-triggered analysis of two-photon imaging data shown in Figure 3H and citation to Bryant et al., 2010.

claim: In lobule simplex, the peak of the pre-reward Cspks occurred at nearly the same time relative to the cue on trials with early (300 ms) as compared to late licks (330 ms).
source: Specifically, we averaged trials with the earliest and latest quartiles of licking. This analysis revealed that the peak of the pre-reward Cspks occurred at nearly the same time relative to the cue on trials with early as compared to late licks (Cspk latency on early trials: 300 ms; late trials: 330 ms), and with similar, but slightly smaller, amplitude (p=4.4×10−4; n = 906 dendrites, 16 mice, paired t-test; Figure 3I).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of two-photon imaging data segregated by lick timing shown in Figure 3I.

claim: In lobule simplex, Cspk responses had identical timing (300 ms) on trials with the highest and lowest lick rates.
source: In addition, we also compared trials with the highest and lowest lick rates, and found that Cspk responses had identical timing (high and low lick rate Cspk latency = 300 ms; Figure 3J) and a qualitatively similar, though statistically different amplitude prior to reward delivery (p=7.4×10−05, paired t-test; Figure 3J).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of two-photon imaging data segregated by lick rate shown in Figure 3J.

claim: In Crus I, pre-learning Cspk activity was sensory-related and followed the visual cue at a time well before reward delivery or licking on both rewarded (p=3.6×10−20, n = 133 dendrites, six mice) and omission trials (p=3.4×10−17).
source: In Crus I, pre-learning Cspk activity differed substantially from LS. Specifically, in naïve animals, Cspk activity was sensory-related, and followed the visual cue at a time well before reward delivery or licking on both rewarded (p=3.6×10−20, n = 133 dendrites, six mice; one-tailed t-test; Figure 5A,D) and omission trials (p=3.4×10−17).
evidence: This is supported by two-photon imaging data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 5A and 5D.

claim: In Crus I, after learning, Cspk responses to the visual cue were significantly enhanced (p=2.3×10−8, n = 178 dendrites, seven mice).
source: After learning, however, once the cue had been associated with upcoming reward, Cspk responses to the visual cue were significantly enhanced (p=2.3×10−8, unpaired t-test, n = 178 dendrites, seven mice; Figure 5B,C,E).
evidence: This is supported by two-photon imaging data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 5B, 5C, and 5E.

claim: In Crus I, there were only weak or non-significant reward responses on rewarded or omission trials, either before (rewarded: p=0.002; omission: p=0.21) or after learning (rewarded: p=1.0; omission: p=0.84).
source: In contrast, there were only weak or non-significant reward responses on rewarded or omission trials, either before (rewarded: p=0.002; omission: p=0.21; one-tailed t-test; Figure 5D,E) or after learning (rewarded: p=1.0; omission: p=0.84; one-tailed t-test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of two-photon imaging data shown in Figure 5D and 5E.

claim: In Crus I, there was no Cspk response to unexpected reward in naïve animals, but a large Cspk response to unexpected reward in the same animals after learning (p=5.1×10−11, n = 141, five mice).
source: Notably, despite the lack of a Cspk response to unexpected reward in naïve animals, there was a large Cspk response to unexpected reward in the same animals after learning (p=5.1×10−11, n = 141, five mice, one-tailed t-test; Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by two-photon imaging data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claim: In Crus I, PC dendrites that were significantly cue responsive (n = 100/141) also showed a robust response to unexpected reward (p=7.7×10−11).
source: To test whether the same PC dendrites that exhibit Cspk responses following the visual cue also respond to unexpected reward, we identified those PC dendrites that were significantly cue responsive. Indeed, these PC dendrites (n = 100/141) also showed a robust response to unexpected reward (p=7.7×10−11; one-tailed t-test; Figure 5G), indicating that PC dendrites can signal expectation under distinct conditions.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of two-photon imaging data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: In Crus I, there was no significant Cspk response to licks during the ITI in naïve animals (p=0.04; n = 93 dendrites, four mice).
source: As further evidence that Cspk responses in Crus I are sensory related in naïve animals, there was no significant Cspk response to licks during the ITI (p=0.04; n = 93 dendrites, four mice, one-tailed t-test; Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by lick-triggered analysis of two-photon imaging data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: In Crus I, the timing (230 ms) and amplitude (p=0.04) of Cspk activity following the visual cue was largely independent of lick timing.
source: To test whether licking contributes to the learned increase in response amplitude following the cue, we segregated trials according to the timing of the first lick. This revealed that the timing (early and late lick Cspk latency: 230 ms) and amplitude (p=0.04, paired t-test; Figure 5I) of Cspk activity following the visual cue was largely independent of lick timing.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of two-photon imaging data segregated by lick timing shown in Figure 5I.

claim: In Crus I, the amount of licking did not alter the timing (230 ms) or amplitude (p=0.4) of pre-reward Cspk responses.
source: In addition, we also compared trials with the highest and lowest lick rates, and found the amount of licking also did not alter the timing (high and low lick rate Cspk latency: 230 ms) or amplitude of pre-reward Cspk responses (p=0.4, paired t-test; Figure 5J).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of two-photon imaging data segregated by lick rate shown in Figure 5J.

claim: In Crus II, Cspk rates were elevated in response to reward delivery in naïve animals (p=2.7×10−18; n = 147 dendrites, five mice), but not on reward omission trials (p=1.0).
source: Finally, we measured Cspk activity in Crus II. Similar to area LS, Cspk rates were elevated in response to reward delivery in naïve animals (p=2.7×10−18; n = 147 dendrites, five mice, one-tailed t-test; Figure 6A,D), but not on reward omission trials (p=1.0).
evidence: This is supported by two-photon imaging data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 6A and 6D.

claim: In Crus II, after learning, a robust cue response was observed on both rewarded (p=9.7×10−26; n = 245 dendrites, n = 6 mice) and omission trials (p=6.1×10−21).
source: After learning, a robust cue response was observed in Crus II on both rewarded (p=9.7×10−26; n = 245 dendrites, n = 6 mice, one-tailed t-test; Figure 6B,C,E) and omission trials (p=6.1×10−21).
evidence: This is supported by two-photon imaging data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 6B, 6C, and 6E.

claim: In Crus II, the reward response persisted after learning (p=5.6×10−11).
source: However, distinct from area LS, the reward response persisted after learning (p=5.6×10−11; Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by two-photon imaging data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 6E.

claim: In Crus II, there was no significantly increased Cspk response on omission trials at the time of expected reward after learning (p=0.95).
source: However, we observed no significantly increased response on omission trials at the time of expected reward (p=0.95); nor did we observe any significant suppression.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of two-photon imaging data.

claim: In Crus II, when reward was delivered unexpectedly after learning, enhanced Cspk rates were observed as compared to the Cspk responses to expected reward (p=1.1×10−11, n = 184 dendrites, six mice).
source: When reward was delivered unexpectedly after learning, we observed enhanced Cspk rates as compared to the Cspk responses to expected reward (p=1.1×10−11, n = 184 dendrites, six mice; Figure 6F), suggesting a component of the learned response that scales with expectation.
evidence: This is supported by two-photon imaging data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 6F.

claim: In Crus II, the same PC dendrites that respond to the cue after learning (n = 60/184) continue to respond to both the expected (p=1.5×10−4) and unexpected reward (p=1.1×10−15) after learning.
source: Notably, the same PC dendrites that respond to the cue after learning (n = 60/184) continue to respond to both the expected (p=1.5×10−4; one-tailed t-test; Figure 6G) and unexpected reward (p=1.1×10−15) after learning.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of two-photon imaging data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: In Crus II, in naïve animals there was a significant lick related response as measured by the lick triggered average of Cspk activity during the ITI (p=1.6×10−5, n = 104).
source: In contrast with area LS and Crus I, in naïve animals we observed a significant lick related response in Crus II as measured by the lick triggered average of Cspk activity during the ITI (p=1.6×10−5, n = 104; one-tailed t-test; Figure 6H).
evidence: This is supported by lick-triggered analysis of two-photon imaging data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: In Crus II, lick-related Cspk responses disappeared after learning (p=0.98; n = 136 dendrites, three mice).
source: Interestingly, however, these responses disappeared after learning (p=0.98; n = 136 dendrites, three mice).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of two-photon imaging data.

claim: In Crus II, after learning, the pre-reward timing of Cspks was independent of lick timing (Cspk latency on both early and late lick trials = 300 ms).
source: Moreover, after learning, the pre-reward timing of Cspks was independent of lick timing (Cspk latency on both early and late lick trials = 300 ms; Figure 6I), and Cspks maintained a similar rate following the cue (p=0.002; paired t-test; Figure 6I) regardless of lick timing.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of two-photon imaging data segregated by lick timing shown in Figure 6I.

claim: In Crus II, the amount of licking did not alter the timing of Cspk responses (high and low lick rate Cspk latency = 300 ms).
source: In addition, we also compared trials with the highest and lowest lick rates, and found the amount of licking also did not alter the timing of Cspk responses (high and low lick rate Cspk latency = 300 ms; Figure 6J), and produced Cspk responses with similar though statistically different amplitude prior to reward (p=4.1×10−5, paired t-test; Figure 6J).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of two-photon imaging data segregated by lick rate shown in Figure 6J.

claim: There was no relationship between the learned Cspk response and movement in LS (p=0.13, n = 316 dendrites, five mice), Crus I (p=0.13, n = 27 dendrites, two mice), or Crus II (p=0.10, n = 97 dendrites, three mice).
source: Using this approach, we segregated trials according to the most and least movement on trial-by-trial basis, and found no relationship between the learned Cspk response and movement (High vs low movement Cspk responses, LS: p=0.13, n = 316 dendrites, five mice; Crus I: p=0.13, n = 27 dendrites, two mice; Crus II: p=0.10, n = 97 dendrites, three mice; Figure 7C–E).
evidence: This is supported by analysis using piezoelectric sensor data shown in Figure 7C-E.

claim: Climbing fibers in LS can carry somatosensory input related to forelimbs.
source: For example, climbing fibers in LS can carry somatosensory input related to forelimbs (Apps and Garwicz, 2005), but also exhibit responses consistent with reinforcement learning signals (Heffley et al., 2018; Kostadinov et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Apps and Garwicz, 2005.

claim: Climbing fibers in LS exhibit responses consistent with reinforcement learning signals.
source: For example, climbing fibers in LS can carry somatosensory input related to forelimbs (Apps and Garwicz, 2005), but also exhibit responses consistent with reinforcement learning signals (Heffley et al., 2018; Kostadinov et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Heffley et al., 2018; Kostadinov et al., 2019.

claim: Crus I climbing fibers can carry diverse sensory input related to visual, auditory and somatosensory stimuli.
source: Crus I climbing fibers can carry diverse sensory input related to visual, auditory and somatosensory stimuli (Gaffield et al., 2019; Ju et al., 2019), and Crus II climbing fibers can respond during various motor behaviors such as licking and whisker movement (Brown and Raman, 2018; Gaffield et al., 2016; Gaffield and Christie, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Gaffield et al., 2019; Ju et al., 2019.

claim: Crus II climbing fibers can respond during various motor behaviors such as licking and whisker movement.
source: Crus I climbing fibers can carry diverse sensory input related to visual, auditory and somatosensory stimuli (Gaffield et al., 2019; Ju et al., 2019), and Crus II climbing fibers can respond during various motor behaviors such as licking and whisker movement (Brown and Raman, 2018; Gaffield et al., 2016; Gaffield and Christie, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Brown and Raman, 2018; Gaffield et al., 2016; Gaffield and Christie, 2017.

claim: The lateral cerebellum has been implicated in non-motor behaviors.
source: However, these lateral cerebellar regions have also been implicated in non-motor behaviors (Badura et al., 2018; Carta et al., 2019; Deverett et al., 2018; Schmahmann et al., 2019), and with cognitive deficits such as autism spectrum disorders (Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Badura et al., 2018; Carta et al., 2019; Deverett et al., 2018; Schmahmann et al., 2019.

claim: The lateral cerebellum has connectivity to the anterior cingulate cortex, prefrontal cortex, and orbitofrontal cortex.
source: Such contributions to cognitive processes may be enabled by connectivity from these cerebellar regions to downstream targets such as the anterior cingulate cortex, prefrontal cortex, orbitofrontal cortex (Badura et al., 2018), hippocampus (Hoshi et al., 2005; McAfee et al., 2019) and striatum (Hoshi et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Badura et al., 2018.

claim: The lateral cerebellum has connectivity to the hippocampus.
source: Such contributions to cognitive processes may be enabled by connectivity from these cerebellar regions to downstream targets such as the anterior cingulate cortex, prefrontal cortex, orbitofrontal cortex (Badura et al., 2018), hippocampus (Hoshi et al., 2005; McAfee et al., 2019) and striatum (Hoshi et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Hoshi et al., 2005; McAfee et al., 2019.

claim: The lateral cerebellum has connectivity to the striatum.
source: Such contributions to cognitive processes may be enabled by connectivity from these cerebellar regions to downstream targets such as the anterior cingulate cortex, prefrontal cortex, orbitofrontal cortex (Badura et al., 2018), hippocampus (Hoshi et al., 2005; McAfee et al., 2019) and striatum (Hoshi et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Hoshi et al., 2005.

claim: Cspk responses to licking are localized primarily to Crus II.
source: Here, by imaging naïve animals, we were able to demonstrate no significant lick response in absence of learning in area LS and Crus I, consistent with previous reports indicating Cspk responses to licking are localized primarily to Crus II (Gaffield et al., 2016; Gaffield et al., 2018; Welsh et al., 1995).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Gaffield et al., 2016; Gaffield et al., 2018; Welsh et al., 1995.

claim: Output from the lateral cerebellum via the deep cerebellar nuclei (DCN) forms a monosynaptic, excitatory connection onto dopamine neurons in the VTA.
source: In particular, a recent study has demonstrated that output from the lateral cerebellum via the deep cerebellar nuclei (DCN) forms a monosynaptic, excitatory connection onto dopamine neurons in the VTA (Carta et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Carta et al., 2019.

claim: Activating DCN projections to the VTA is sufficient to positively modulate reward-driven behaviors.
source: Activating these DCN projections is sufficient to positively modulate reward-driven behaviors, and these same projections are endogenously active under social conditions.
evidence: This statement refers to findings from Carta et al., 2019 mentioned in the previous sentence.

claim: DCN projections to the VTA are endogenously active under social conditions.
source: Activating these DCN projections is sufficient to positively modulate reward-driven behaviors, and these same projections are endogenously active under social conditions.
evidence: This statement refers to findings from Carta et al., 2019 mentioned in the previous sentence.

claim: The learned Cspk responses are driven by the reward-predictive visual cue, and not reafference or sensory feedback related to movement.
source: These data strongly support the hypothesis that the learned Cspk responses demonstrated here are driven by the reward-predictive visual cue, and not reafference or sensory feedback related to movement.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the piezoelectric sensor data showing no relationship between movement and Cspk responses.

claim: In all three lateral cerebellar areas (LS, Crus I, Crus II), there was a learned Cspk response related to reward prediction.
source: Specifically, in LS and Crus II, Cspk responses emerged as a function of learning to a cue that predicted upcoming reward. In Crus I, while a sensory-evoked Cspk response to the visual cue was already evident in naïve animals, this response was enhanced once the cue had been associated with upcoming reward. Hence, in all three areas, there was a learned Cspk response related to reward prediction.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the experimental findings presented in the results section.

claim: In LS, the response to expected reward was largely lost after learning, but was pronounced when reward was delivered unexpectedly.
source: In LS, the response to expected reward was largely lost after learning, but was pronounced when reward was delivered unexpectedly.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the experimental findings presented in the results section.

claim: In Crus I, while there was no reward response in naïve animals, a Cspk response to unexpected reward emerged only after the animals established an expectation of reward delivery in response to the visual cue.
source: In Crus I, while there was no reward response in naïve animals, a Cspk response to unexpected reward emerged only after the animals established an expectation of reward delivery in response to the visual cue.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the experimental findings presented in the results section.

claim: In Crus II, reward responses persisted across learning, even after a separate Cspk response emerged to the reward-predictive visual cue.
source: Finally, in Crus II, reward responses persisted across learning, even after a separate Cspk response emerged to the reward-predictive visual cue.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the experimental findings presented in the results section.

claim: The post-learning Cspk response to unexpected reward in Crus II was enhanced, as compared to trials when reward was expected.
source: The post-learning Cspk response to unexpected reward was enhanced, however, as compared to trials when reward was expected.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the experimental findings presented in the results section.

claim: The learned changes in Cspk responses in each lateral cerebellar area are overlaid on the unique sensory and motor Cspk signals pre-existing in each region.
source: The differences in responses, however, also suggest that learned changes in each area are overlaid on the unique sensory and motor Cspk signals pre-existing in each region.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observed differences in Cspk responses across the three areas.

claim: The lateral cerebellum can harness distinct sensory and motor signals across each area for different forms of sensorimotor learning.
source: Thus, these data also indicate that the lateral cerebellum can harness other distinct sensory and motor signals across each area for different forms of sensorimotor learning, and perhaps to utilize alternate learning strategies that depend on task requirements.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observed functional compartmentalization of Cspk responses.

claim: The same climbing fibers that respond to reward in naïve animals can instead respond to a reward predictive cue after learning.
source: Imaging Cspk activity across learning suggests that the same climbing fibers that respond to reward in naïve animals can instead respond to a reward predictive cue after learning.
evidence: This is supported by the tracking experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: There is no evidence of negative prediction error following reward omission immediately after learning.
source: Finally, we observe no evidence of negative prediction error following reward omission immediately after learning, suggesting the possibility that Cspk responses may not instruct a strict temporal difference (TD) learning model in this paradigm.
evidence: This is based on the absence of suppressed Cspk responses at the time of expected reward on omission trials.

claim: Cspk responses may not instruct a strict temporal difference (TD) learning model in this paradigm.
source: Finally, we observe no evidence of negative prediction error following reward omission immediately after learning, suggesting the possibility that Cspk responses may not instruct a strict temporal difference (TD) learning model in this paradigm.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the absence of negative prediction errors.

claim: The learned, reward-predictive Cspk signals are consistent with a model that would allow learned cerebellar output to provide information about rewarding stimuli to downstream structures such as the VTA and striatum.
source: The learned, reward predictive Cspk signals observed here are, however, consistent with a model that would allow learned cerebellar output to provide information about rewarding stimuli to downstream structures such as the VTA and striatum.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observed Cspk responses and known connectivity.

claim: Mesoscale calcium imaging of Purkinje cell dendrites expressing GCaMP6f accurately reports Cspk activity.
source: This method has previously been demonstrated to accurately report Cspk activity (Heffley et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Heffley et al., 2018.

claim: Calcium transient amplitude variability in PC dendrites reflects the properties of climbing fiber input, and not a combined climbing fiber and parallel fiber signal.
source: Previous work has demonstrated that calcium transient amplitude variability reflects the properties of climbing fiber input, and not a combined climbing fiber and parallel fiber signal (Gaffield et al., 2019; Gaffield et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Gaffield et al., 2019; Gaffield et al., 2018.

claim: In the mesolimbic dopamine system, dopamine release is governed by correct movement initiation, and not simply reward prediction.
source: In support of a role for task-specific movement requirements is shaping instructional signals, in the mesolimbic dopamine system it has been shown with a similar operant task that dopamine release is governed by correct movement initiation, and not simply reward prediction (Syed et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Syed et al., 2016.

claim: In VTA dopamine neurons, increased firing to reward can persist after learning.
source: Lastly, recent measurements of VTA dopamine neuron responses have revealed that increased firing to reward can persist after learning (Coddington and Dudman, 2018), similar to what we observe in Crus II.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Coddington and Dudman, 2018.

claim: In VTA dopamine neurons, negative prediction errors emerge very late in training, indicating that over-training can be required for omission responses to develop.
source: In those experiments, negative prediction errors did emerge eventually, but only very late in training, indicating that over-training can be required for omission responses to develop.
evidence: This statement refers to findings from Coddington and Dudman, 2018 mentioned in the previous sentence.

claim: VTA dopamine neurons have different response profiles depending on their striatal projection target.
source: Another possibility is suggested by the mesolimbic dopamine system, where neurons have different response profiles depending on their striatal projection target (Menegas et al., 2017; Parker et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Menegas et al., 2017; Parker et al., 2016.

claim: Climbing fibers may exhibit target-specific response variability and signal diverse reward-related information in different regions of the cerebellum.
source: It thus remains possible that climbing fibers also exhibit an analogous target-specific response variability, and signal diverse reward-related information such as negative prediction errors in other regions of the cerebellum.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on analogy to the VTA dopamine system.

claim: Learned, reward-predictive climbing fiber signals are ideally suited to instruct both cerebellar learning and modulation of reward processing in downstream brain regions.
source: These learned, reward-predictive climbing fiber signals are ideally suited to instruct both cerebellar learning and modulation of reward processing in downstream brain regions (Chabrol et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observed Cspk responses, with citation to Chabrol et al., 2019.

claim: Cspk instructional signals can become associated with stimuli that predict reward.
source: Specifically, we have shown Cspk instructional signals can become associated with stimuli that predict reward.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the experimental findings.

claim: Cspk signals combined with contextual information from the mossy fiber pathway would be effective in instructing plasticity to depress Purkinje cell output and enable DCN output to the VTA in response to reward-associated stimuli or actions.
source: If combined with contextual information from the mossy fiber pathway, such Cspk signals would be effective in instructing plasticity to depress Purkinje cell output and thereby enable DCN output to the VTA in response to any new, earlier reward-associated stimuli or actions.
evidence: This is a speculative model based on the observed Cspk responses and known cerebellar circuitry.
